findings.summary: The restore-chain information is spread across the table and two trailing bullets, and the table cell for differential is vaguer than the cheat sheet.
findings.evidence:
Differential | changes since last full | full + differential (2 sets)
...
Differential: grows daily, restores with just 2 sets
findings.fix: Add 'Backup size/speed' and 'Restore speed' columns to the table and drop the two trailing bullets. Write 'full + latest differential' to match page 6.

findings.summary: The PITR recipe omits restore_command, which PostgreSQL needs to fetch archived WAL during recovery, so the steps shown would not replay anything from /archive.
findings.evidence:
archive_command = 'cp %p /archive/%f'
# restore base backup, then in postgresql.conf:
recovery_target_time = '2026-10-28 14:05:00'
touch $PGDATA/recovery.signal
findings.fix: Add restore_command = 'cp /archive/%f %p' to the recovery settings alongside recovery_target_time. Optionally add recovery_target_action.

findings.summary: The PostgreSQL PITR example sets a recovery target but never tells the server how to fetch the archived WAL, so the steps would not replay anything.
findings.evidence: "archive_command = 'cp %p /archive/%f'" is followed by "recovery_target_time = '2026-10-28 14:05:00'" and "touch $PGDATA/recovery.signal", with no restore_command.
findings.fix: Add "restore_command = 'cp /archive/%f %p'" next to recovery_target_time, and say that it is what reads the archived WAL back during recovery.

findings.summary: The PITR code block comes before the one-line idea behind it is stated as a process, and it mixes a config line, a comment and prose in one bash block.
findings.evidence:
bash
archive_command = 'cp %p /archive/%f'
# restore base backup, then in postgresql.conf:
recovery_target_time = '2026-10-28 14:05:00'
touch $PGDATA/recovery.signal
start the server; it replays WAL up to the target
findings.fix: Show PITR as a short flow diagram (Base backup -> Replay WAL -> Stop at target), as page 6 does. Keep only the real config lines in the code block and move 'start the server; it replays WAL' out into a bullet.

findings.summary: One bullet holds several ideas: how WAL is shipped, what to set, and the recovery.signal step.
findings.evidence: PostgreSQL: archive_command ships WAL; set the target, add recovery.signal, start
findings.fix: Split into separate bullets: archive_command ships WAL; set recovery_target_time; create recovery.signal and start the server.

findings.summary: The term 'losers' is used on the first page of ARIES without being defined.
findings.evidence: "Repeat history during redo, even for losers" appears before "Undo: roll back losers, write CLRs", and neither line says that losers are the transactions that were uncommitted at the crash.
findings.fix: Define it at first use: "losers = transactions that were still uncommitted at the crash; winners = those that committed."

findings.summary: The 'Needs' column is cryptic for a skimming reader: it does not say which log (undo or redo) each buffer policy requires.
findings.evidence:
Steal | Dirty pages of uncommitted txns may reach disk | Undo
No-force | Commit does not force pages to disk | Redo
findings.fix: Change the column to 'Needs' -> 'So recovery needs', with 'Undo log to roll back' and 'Redo log to replay'.

findings.summary: A bullet holds two ideas: redo skipping and pageLSN storage, plus the LSN definition.
findings.evidence: Every log record has an LSN; each page stores its pageLSN
findings.fix: Split into 'Every log record has an LSN' and 'Each page stores its pageLSN; redo skips a record when pageLSN >= LSN'.

findings.summary: The mistakes section has a malformed bullet and one that holds two ideas.
findings.evidence: Never restore-testing backups or rehearsing failover
findings.fix: Reword as a mistake heading, 'Never restore-testing backups or rehearsing failover' -> 'Skipping restore tests and failover drills'. Keep 'An untested backup is not a backup' as its own line.

findings.summary: The table implies FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY makes superusers subject to RLS, but superusers (and roles with BYPASSRLS) always bypass it.
findings.evidence: Owner, superuser | bypass RLS unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY
findings.fix: Write: 'Table owner bypasses RLS unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set; superusers and BYPASSRLS roles always bypass it.'
